question: Consider a long current carrying solenoid. If Rahul plots the magnetic field lines inside this long current carrying solenoid, then it appears:

options.text: denser to increase from one end to another

solution:
The correct answer is __**uniform at all points**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In a long current-carrying solenoid, the magnetic field inside is **uniform** and parallel to the axis of the solenoid.
 
• The magnetic field lines inside the solenoid are **equally spaced**, indicating a constant magnetic field.
 
• The field outside the solenoid is weak and **non-uniform** compared to the field inside.
 
• The **strength of the magnetic field** inside a solenoid is directly proportional to the number of turns per unit length and the current passing through the solenoid.
 
• For an ideal long solenoid, the edge effects are negligible, and the magnetic field is considered uniform throughout the length of the solenoid.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Magnetic Field Lines**

 
 
• These are imaginary lines used to represent the strength and direction of a magnetic field.
 
 
• **Electromagnetism**
 
 
• It is the interaction between electricity and magnetism.
 
• A current-carrying conductor generates a magnetic field around it.
 
• Electromagnets are widely used in various applications like motors, transformers, and relays.
 
 
 
• **Solenoid Applications**
 
 
• Solenoids are used in devices that require controlled magnetic fields, such as electromechanical relays and solenoid valves.
 
• They are also used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines.
 
• Solenoids are integral components in many industrial applications, including automation and control systems.
